text:
Chapter Nineteen


The ceremony concluded without any interruption from wailing banshees or wandering ghouls, and Maggie’s cheeks were sore from so much smiling. At every turn, Arthur Taliesin was surprising her. She had been delighted by his candid speech and relished in the student reactions around her. She felt a secret thrill that she already knew this Taliesin because he’d let her in before anyone else.


She was walking through the crowd, turning around every now and then to see if she could see him through the throng, but she got caught up in the swell of people with Dahlia. Every other year, this was when Dahlia and Maggie would return to Ilex Hall and unearth a dusty bottle of liquor from one of their desk drawers to give a final toast to the year, but instead they decided to walk the long way past Ilex Hall toward Maggie’s apartment to have their end-of-the-year drink there.


They stepped over the rope sectioning off this part of campus from curious family members, and stopped beneath the hawthorn, tossing their caps onto one of the picnic tables. They watched the swirling miasma on the third floor, tinted purple and glimmering, shadows skating past the windows that sent shivers down Maggie’s spine.


“What a weird end to the year,” Dahlia muttered as she looked up at the third floor. Maggie was quiet, watching the pall intently. Did it seem stronger? Brighter? She had been here yesterday, but she couldn’t remember if she had glanced upward, realizing with a strange sinking in her stomach that she was starting to get used to the way the otherworldly magic had infiltrated campus. But there was something about how the pall seemed to press against the windows that made the hair on her arms stand on end.


“Dahlia—” Maggie began, reaching out to touch her friend’s regalia at her elbow.


At the same time, Dahlia said, “Something is wrong.”


They watched as the pall moved, looking more alive than before, and the lights flickered. When they came on, they lit the wards Taliesin had drawn, and she could see it now. Fracture lines in the liquid chalk, cracks visible even from here.


“The wards are failing,” Maggie gasped. If those wards failed, the pall would no longer be contained. It would fill every inch of Ilex Hall, becoming more of a beacon for fantasmia and, maybe, continuing to grow even beyond the building. She didn’t even know what happened if a pall grew larger than a building. She had to find Taliesin, and she had to find him now. She tore off toward the graduation ceremony, Dahlia not far behind, leaving their caps on the table, forgotten.



—


Maggie hung up her regalia on the back of their office door as Arthur filled the canister of a chalk pen, tucking it into the inside pocket of his tweed jacket. He filled the next and tossed it to Maggie, who put it in her cardigan pocket.


Maggie’s phone buzzed, and she opened it to see frantic, mothering texts from Dahlia, who had finally gone home after Taliesin and Maggie had begged her. You will text me the instant you are out of that pall. If I don’t hear from you by 9, I will come in there myself. Maggie responded with promises to call her later, and put the phone in her desk drawer. It wouldn’t work within the pall anyway; the otherworldly surge of magic would fry the spelltech.


Taliesin was strangely silent, and she could feel his unease. He fidgeted about the room, looking for something to do with his hands, and settled on buttoning and unbuttoning his jacket. “Do you have anything we can use as a face covering?” he asked, and she found two old T-shirts from club days, tossing Taliesin the Hawthorn Hummingbirds a cappella shirt and keeping the Tarot Team shirt for herself.


Maggie couldn’t quite find the same energy to be nervous herself. She brimmed with something like excitement, though she understood the danger they would be in. She wanted to see the pall that had undone Arthur Taliesin so thoroughly; she wanted to see what kind of magic it was that he couldn’t tame. There was a bitter part of her that maybe wanted to see if she could be the one who could tame it instead.


“Maggie,” Taliesin began. “There’s something I need to tell you.” He ran his hands through his hair and pushed his glasses up the bridge of his nose. “I should have…” He paused, and then he sighed.


“What is it?”


“The third floor is swarmed with unsettled dead.”


“I know that,” she said, could hear and feel the faint reverberation of their energy even now. “I’ll be careful.”


“No,” he said. “You have to promise me. Promise me you won’t let one touch you.”


Like the pall itself, a touch from one of the unsettled dead could affect a person’s mental state. Maggie knew that, but she didn’t quite understand Taliesin’s fear. “I’ve read—”


“It’s nothing like what you’ve read,” he interrupted her, his voice harsh. “Just trust me. Promise me.”


She narrowed her eyes, but then said, “Okay, I promise.”


Finally, when there was nothing else they could prepare, Taliesin sighed again. “Let’s get this over with.”



—


The first thing Maggie noticed when she entered the pall wasn’t the way the chill seemed to take up residence in her chest or the strange, viscous quality of the atmosphere. It was the slight pressure of Taliesin’s hand on the small of her back. It wasn’t the smell of ether, sulfuric and bitter, but the subtle spice of his cologne lingering on her skin after he’d leaned over to deactivate the same rune he’d drawn the day the pall fell. They slipped through the door, one after the other, as quickly as possible so none of the otherworldly particles or the slime that seemed to pulse with life could escape. Once inside, Maggie placed her hand on top of Taliesin’s and whispered the Diadhan word for seal to keep the pall from spreading until they left.


Maggie didn’t let her hand linger on top of Taliesin’s, instead tugging up the T-shirt she’d tied around her neck. Taliesin followed suit, covering his mouth and nose against the dust and debris floating around them, against the particles of unseen elements that could burrow in the body. Maggie made a move to walk down the hall, but then Taliesin grabbed her elbow. “Maggie, wait,” he said with a stern edge to his voice. “We are going to fix the wards and go. I don’t want you in here any longer than you need to be.” She couldn’t see half of his face behind the covering, but his eyes were pleading. Worried. “Stay by my side. Time is different in here.”


Unexpected pleasure coiled through her at his concern, cutting through whatever nerves she felt about the pall around her. She searched for something witty to say back, something about how bossy he was being, but the only embarrassing thought in her head was that she might like it. Instead, she just nodded.


Maggie had read all of Taliesin’s reports from front to back, poring over the details of each page until she was confident she could face this, but it was different seeing it in person. It was different being within the thrall of this nightmare. Everything had a quality of unreality that Maggie couldn’t quite explain, as if her brain couldn’t process what she was seeing and feeling and hearing. Fractured beams of sunlight from outside filtered through deep purple, turning her skin a shadowed mauve. The faefire lamps still flickered above them, casting eerie shapes as they blinked off and on. The air felt thick, something to swim through, and pall slime coated the floor. Maggie wondered idly if it would soak through her shoes.


The flotsam and jetsam of that final day of classes floated aimlessly. A metal measuring tool flew by, faster than Maggie thought it should, and she reached out to touch it, changing its trajectory through the miasma. It careened into a wall, its metal pieces striking together and creating a reverberating clang that startled them both. Maggie was sure she could see the sound waves as they moved through the clouds of otherworldly dust, and she couldn’t stop staring.


“There are thirty warded windows on this floor.” Taliesin’s voice interrupted her reverie. “We need to move quickly.”


“Let’s start in 309,” Maggie suggested, just as a paper advertising the campus Beltane fair floated by. Beltane seemed so far away here, a dream of a night while now she was stuck in a nightmare. Maggie led the way, but Taliesin was close behind her, his head turning from side to side. “What are you looking for?” she whispered.


“The unsettled dead,” he said. “Can’t you hear them?” Just above the baseline static that seemed to accompany the pall there was a faint, hum-like moan. These were not the fantasmia plaguing Galloway—not a wraith, ghoul, or banshee—but once-settled souls who temporarily found themselves back on this plane. They were confused and desperate to return to their rest, and somehow all of it was contained in the melancholy sound they made. The sound seemed to burrow in her chest.


“C’mon,” she said. “Let’s go.”


Classroom 309 was frozen in time. Chairs were knocked over, and anything lighter than a pencil was at risk of taking flight. The warding runes were drawn on the row of windows at the back of the classroom. As she made her way around toppled desks, Maggie caught her reflection in the glass and saw that even her hair had lifted from her shoulders, spreading behind her like a strange coronet.


She shook her chalk pen to mix the liquid inside. The tiny fissures where the magic entrapping the pall had weakened glowed, illuminated from behind by the afternoon sun. She held her chalk pen to the rune and began tracing Taliesin’s sure lines, adjusting the shape slightly to account for the new date and time. At the opposite end of the line of windows, he began the same task.


She traced the next warding rune as she waited for the last to dry. When she was convinced the chalk wouldn’t smear, she went back to say the Diadhan incantation with her fingers grazing the symbol. It glowed faintly as she finished the spell. She did another. And then another.


At the last of her runes, as she pressed her fingers against the window, she looked through Taliesin’s precise lines and the glass they were written on and was strangely grateful to see the real world was still outside, sunlight making its way through heavy clouds and down to the lawn below. But through the purple tinge the pall left over everything, it felt like a world Maggie couldn’t touch. A small voice in her mind asked quietly if she would ever touch it again. Would she ever feel warm sunlight on her cheek? The softest brush of clover beneath bare feet? The gods-sent relief of a breeze on a hot day? Would the world ever be hers again?


That single thought bloomed into a sadness that fell over Maggie like a shroud. She plucked her hand from the rune and swallowed the Diadhan words she had been about to say, lest she feed the pall around her, but that was all she could manage before anguish took root in her chest. She gasped. It was a sadness so profound that it hurt. It was a sorrow deeper than any she’d ever felt before.


Even though he had been on the other side of the room, somehow Taliesin knew something was wrong, because not a moment passed before he was at her side. His large hands cradled her cheeks, and he bent until their faces were nose to nose. “What happened? Are you all right?”


“I’m—” she said, and her cheeks began to heat as she felt inexplicable tears building in her eyes. Gods below, was she going to cry in front of Taliesin again? “What’s wrong with me?” she asked, her voice meek.


“It’s the pall,” he reminded her. “It can affect your emotions.”


Melancholia. Maggie wondered why she had never given that particular side effect another thought. It had always seemed so secondary to every other symptom of pall sickness, but gods, she was wrong. Why had Taliesin never told her? It was every sad thought she’d ever had, multiplied. Every grief, expanded. Tears welled. “This is horrible,” she sputtered, her nose getting snotty. “How did you bear it?”


Something flashed across Taliesin’s features, and she could tell he went somewhere else, lost in a memory of something he didn’t share with her. “The first two times, not well,” he admitted. “It took days for the sadness to lift.”


“And the third?”


Their noses were nearly touching, and there was something comforting about the angles of his face, something warm in his amber-colored eyes. The pall fell away, if only for a moment. She couldn’t see his lips behind the makeshift mask, but she imagined they curved into a sad smile as his eyes crinkled, just a bit. “The third time, I had someone berate me about vomiting on her couch, and I forgot to be sad.”


Oh, she thought, remembering the way she had yelled at him that day, unaware of the dread and exhaustion and sorrow that must have been plaguing him. “I’m so sorry,” she said, and the tears began to fall in a steady stream down her cheeks.


“I’m not.” His voice was so soft, but somehow it cut through the otherworldly sounds of the pall. He brushed away her tears with the calloused pad of his thumb before they could collect in the fabric of her mask. Without thinking, she leaned into his touch.


Relief. It was so immediate, her breath caught in her throat as the melancholia lightened, if only a little bit. When she looked up at Taliesin, his eyes widened slightly, as if, somehow, he felt it, too. The shock of whatever part of her had found comfort in his touch shook off more of the melancholia. She stood up straight, stepping out of his grip and rubbing her cheeks with her sleeve until they were raw. He straightened, too. “Better?” he asked.


“Yes.” Then, softer, she added, “Thank you.” They both returned to the runes they’d been repairing, completing each spell before moving on to the next. They moved through rooms 310 and 311 quickly.


The closer they got to room 312, the worse everything felt. The shroud of melancholia still weighed on her shoulders, heavy. The air felt thicker, the shadows deeper, and the moans of the unsettled had turned reverberant in her chest. Beside her, Taliesin was nervously shaking his chalk pen. “How are you feeling?” she asked him.


“I’m fine.” His voice was as tense and tight as his shoulders, and his gaze was fixed on the open door to room 312.


“This is your fourth time in the pall. Are you feeling any signs of pall sickness?”


Finally, he looked at her. “I’m fine,” he repeated, and then turned back to look at the entrance to his lab. “C’mon.”


The faefire lamps inside flashed even brighter than the ones in the hall. From somewhere within the lab, a rushing roar like a train sounded. Maggie reached out and gave his hand a squeeze. She wasn’t entirely sure what possessed her to do that, but she immediately felt another wave of calm wash over her. Taliesin’s own tense features melted, just slightly.


Then they entered the lab in room 312.


At the front of the classroom, where Taliesin must have been standing when his spell went awry, was the fissure. It looked like a crack in a screen, like the fractured starburst of broken glass. It was on the chalkboard, cutting his rune in half, but it was also floating in the air with nothing behind it. Strange light that Maggie couldn’t quite explain came from the fissure, even though she was looking right at it. It was somehow dark and light all at once. Sparks peeled off the main beam, drifting through the miasma, and Maggie felt a peculiar desire to reach out and touch one of them, but she kept her hands at her sides, balled into fists. Lavender pall slime seeped from the crack, spreading down and out from the fissure and across the floor, pulsing in a simulacrum of breath, of living.


She wanted to stare at it longer, to try to understand what she was seeing, but there was no understanding it. Her mind couldn’t comprehend the way her world had split in two and the next world was spilling through the crack. No logic, no understanding, would make it feel less horrible, less wrong. She pulled herself away from it and returned to her task at the windows with a shudder.


The same tiny cracks spread through the chalk marks in the runes here. She worked as quickly as she could, breathing fast, her lungs aching at the edge of each breath. Nausea bubbled in her stomach, and her head pounded. They had been in here too long already, but there were still six more runes to fortify.


Each stroke of the chalk paint was an effort, each utterance of the incantation drew more from her already depleted body, but they were nearly done. Just as Maggie completed her last rune, nearly whispering the incantation as her voice gave out, there was a crash, and she looked up to see a pair of shears floating through the room, colliding with a desk and coming toward her. Maggie lifted her hand to knock them away as they careened through the miasma, but in that moment, one of those tiny pearls of light that came through the fissure collided with her open palm, exploding in a burst of bright rays.



—


Maggie was here and not here.


She couldn’t tell what was real and not real.


Melancholia bloomed exponentially into an aching, yawning despair. She felt, vaguely, the press of the floor on her side and then nothing, nothing, nothing.



—


Until she felt something again.


It came from the tiny pinprick of light that had flattened against her palm, creating a starburst of beautiful, iridescent shine. It was a life, small and enormous all at once. It was one of the unsettled dead, sucked into Maggie’s world by accident when the pall cracked apart what separates this world from the next.


The now Maggie found herself in was not her own, not at all. It was hers. It was all hers.


She saw the world through unsteady toddler eyes, the warm light of a parent picking her up in their arms. Maggie must have felt so loved, so safe, when she was this small, too, but knowing it was nothing like feeling it again. Before she could grow too comfortable in the sensation, though, it was gone.


Then everything was tinged with an adolescent rage that Maggie hadn’t felt in years but that she put on like an old, worn coat. It felt good. Righteous. It felt strangely like home.


Then she felt the echoes of a dim bar, of a hand on her thigh, whispered words in her ear, and a fluttering, fleeting sense of possibility before it crashed into heartbreak.


This went on and on and on—through first love and first grief, to the expansive love for children and the sweet love for grandchildren, the sudden loneliness of a dying spouse, and more and more and more. The threads of love and loss and joy and anger and so much love tangled in a confusing, comforting knot.


It was overwhelming. It was not hers. And she couldn’t escape it.


She tried to draw herself out of it. She tried to reach for the parts of her that she knew were Maggie. She grasped for the threads, but they were brittle and fraying, and she remembered that thought she’d had in 309. Will I ever see the world again? It was no longer a small voice, instead growing bigger and bigger until she was sure she was lost in this unsettled woman’s memories.


And then there were hands on hers, lacing finger through finger, tethering Maggie to someone, to somewhere. There was the vague notion of her name being called through the ether. She was tugged forward into real and out of the unsettled’s memories, but then she fell back into a childhood memory of red-hot embarrassment.


A whispered voice in her ear. Was it real or not real? Strong arms gripped her back and beneath her legs. She was being lifted, like a child off to bed, her head snug against something soft and hard at once. There was a beat, beat, beat beneath her ear, and it filled her with a feeling so much like home that she nestled into it. This was real, she was certain. She heard a light sound, like a gasp, a quickening of the beat, and then Maggie again knew nothing.


When Maggie woke, she was curled on her fainting couch. The lights were low, only Taliesin’s desk lamp glowed, and she had something thrown over her to keep her warm. Breathing in, she smelled Taliesin’s cologne, and she felt the tattered fabric of his tweed jacket, threadbare and soft. It made her think of the soft beat of his heart, going fast at her touch, at the way she’d nestled in his arms as he cradled her head against him. Not just now, in the pall. But once before, too.


And it was then, finally, that the Beltane spell faded away. Maggie remembered everything.

facts.fact: 典礼后窃喜：她第一个被 Taliesin 请进真实——secret thrill。
惊变：灯闪照出符文裂纹——wards 正在失效；pall 比昨日更亮更活。
facts.anchor: Fracture lines in the liquid chalk

facts.fact: 她狂奔回典礼场找人，毕业帽弃在桌上。
facts.anchor: She tore off toward the graduation ceremony

facts.fact: 准备：Dahlia 九点死线短信；手机带不进 pall（异界浪涌烧 spelltech）；chalk pen 灌满分揣两袋。
他的紧张：解扣又扣上；三楼挤满 unsettled dead——逼她承诺绝不被碰（和读过的不一样）。
入 pall 第一感：不是寒冷黏稠而是他按在她后腰的手；她覆手 whisper 封印词。
pall 内景：空气稠得像游泳、mauve 皮肤、法火忽明灭。
亡者之声：曾安息又被拽回的灵魂，hum 般 moan 钻进胸腔——他们困惑且渴望归位。
melancholia 爆发：309 窗前「我还摸得到世界吗」——悲伤如裹尸布；她咽下咒语防喂养 pall。
他瞬移到她面前捧脸；三次经验：前两次撑得不好，第三次被骂吐脏沙发就忘了难过——解药是她。
光珠击掌：312 实验室 fissure 如星芒悬空；shears 撞桌她抬手挡——tiny pearls of light 之一撞上摊开的掌心爆成光芒。
facts.anchor: tiny pearls of light that came

facts.fact: 灌顶与救援：unsettled 女人的一生灌顶——他十指相扣穿过以太喊她、耳下心跳像家。
章末炸点：她在贵妃榻上醒来盖着他的 tweed——Beltane 咒褪尽，她记起了一切。
